rubric.importance: IT-vs-OT impact (OT process/physical = top), then US energy relevance (subsector + value chain), actor capability, scale, and whether action is possible (patch/hunt beats awareness). Severity on the board is importance.
rubric.correctness: Source tier (A primary/victim, B wire/established press, C vendor research), independent corroboration count, claim-vs-confirmed, and whether the direct source was pulled and matches the outlet. Credibility 1-6 and the Verifier's verdict are correctness.
rubric.rule: Keep the two columns separate. An item can be critical and poorly confirmed (Siemens this week) or fully confirmed and low importance (NCSC forecast). Act on importance, trust on correctness, and say which is which.

severity_scale.critical: OT process or physical/safety impact confirmed or imminent at energy assets, OR an exploited flaw (unauthenticated, remote) in a product that sits in energy OT networks. Action is possible now.
severity_scale.high: OT reached without process effect, or IT impact that forced or could force an operational shutdown, or a law/rule change that alters obligations within weeks, or confirmed exploitation of networking gear used by operators.
severity_scale.medium: IT-only or OT incidents outside energy whose technique transfers directly, or policy with cost/supply-chain effect but no deadline.
severity_scale.low: Forecasts, information operations, or incidents with no transferable technique and no energy victim.
severity_scale.info: Guidance, campaigns and announcements that create no new obligation.

severity_factors: ot_impact (weight 3): none / reached / process affected / physical-safety
us_energy_relevance (weight 2): US energy asset, US operator, or product in US energy networks
actor_capability (weight 1): unattributed low-skill / criminal / state-aligned / state
scale (weight 1): single site / many sites / fleet or sector
actionable (weight 1): patch or hunt available now

reliability_scale.A: primary document, victim statement, government advisory
reliability_scale.B: wire or established press with named sources
reliability_scale.C: vendor research or a firm that sells security products

credibility_scale.2: probably true (one solid source, consistent with others)

rubric.computed_severity: Points from structured fields: OT impact (0-3) x3, US relevance (0-2) x2, actor capability (0-3), scale (0-2), actionable (0-1), exploited/KEV (0-2). Thresholds: critical >=11, high >=7, medium >=4, low >=2, info otherwise. The asserted level may differ from the computed one only with an override_reason.

human_touch.intro: What this society cannot do without a person, and should not pretend to.

items.why: Severity and relevance are scored by rules a person wrote; changing the rules, the weights or the US-first choice is a value judgement. The Ombudsman proposes; the owner decides.
The Counsel can fetch a statute, but deciding what a directive requires of a specific operator is legal judgement, and the text often needs context from counsel who knows the entity.
CISA's feeds and Utility Dive block automated pulls, E-ISAC is members-only, paywalled journals are closed. A person with access has to read those and tell the system what they say.
The most important facts (was OT reached, what did it cost, who was spared) often exist only in a phone call. No agent makes that call.
The cross-check catches a dropped hedge or a wrong CVE; it will not catch a plausible summary that quietly inverts cause and effect. A domain reader will.
The agents quote attributions; they must never make one. Saying 'this was China' or 'this was criminal' with consequences is a human act with accountability attached.
When a briefing is wrong and someone acted on it, a person answers for it. The Ombudsman writes the note; the owner signs it.
Judging whether an outlet is credible enough for the allowlist, and watching it drift, is editorial judgement; the bias notes are a person's opinion, dated.
Historical cases come from the model's memory. Until a person or a scheduled check reads the primary record, they are not evidence.

items.what: Decide whether to publish, to whom, and when.
items.why: Sharing an analysis that names a vendor or a victim has consequences the system cannot weigh. Publishing is a human decision; the page is private until a person shares it.

items.what: Pay for it and set the budget.
items.why: Each run has a measured cost; the choice of model, frequency and depth is a budget decision.
The residents, their names and their jobs were invented by an assistant on a given day; keeping them is a choice, not a fact.

human_touch.automated: What is automated: fetching from the allowlist, relevance filtering, writing briefings and records, pulling direct sources, cross-checking outlet against primary, grading, flagging, logging, exporting, scheduling. The agents start the inquiry without being asked; they do not finish it without a person.

reporter.briefing: Three confirmed incidents at energy companies this week, which is three more than the last run. Peninsula Energy told the ASX a cyber incident at its Wyoming uranium project breached its operating systems and would temporarily affect operations, with administrative systems in the US and Australia unaffected (SecurityWeek, 2026-11-24). KEPCO confirmed a breach of its billing portal and procurement system exposing about 1.5 million customer, representative and employee records, with Korea's privacy regulator confirming an extortion email (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-23; SecurityWeek, 2026-11-24). Norway's NSM linked attacks on two major energy companies, naming Equinor and Skagerak Energi, to a critical Azure API Management flaw Microsoft mitigated on Nov 19 (The Register, 2026-11-23). Osaki Electric, a Japanese smart-meter maker, had production disrupted by ransomware per an OT-ISAC report (Industrial Cyber, 2026-11-24). On the advisory side, CISA published a CVSS 9.8 flaw in Danfoss AK-SM refrigeration controllers and INCIBE a default-credentials advisory for the same family (CISA, 2026-11-24; INCIBE-CERT, 2026-11-23). Claimed, not confirmed: the actor 'Noiem' behind KEPCO.

answers.What happened in energy-sector cyber tod: Peninsula Energy's Wyoming uranium site (operating systems breached, per its own filing), KEPCO's 1.5-million-record breach, two Norwegian energy companies hit through an Azure flaw, and a Japanese smart-meter maker's production halted by ransomware (SecurityWeek, 2026-11-24; BleepingComputer, 2026-11-23; The Register, 2026-11-23; Industrial Cyber, 2026-11-24).
answers.Which US utilities or operators were aff: Peninsula Energy, Lance Project, Wyoming: the only US operator confirmed affected, by its own ASX filing (SecurityWeek, 2026-11-24). No US grid operator, pipeline or refinery reported an incident in the allowlisted feeds.
answers.What is confirmed and what is still only: Confirmed by the victim: Peninsula (incident and scope unstated), KEPCO (breach and counts), GL.iNet (cloud flaw exploited). Confirmed by a government: Norway's NSM on the Azure attacks. Claimed only: 'Noiem' as KEPCO's attacker. Not read directly: the OT-ISAC report on Osaki (the relay blocks our fetch).

reporter.bubble: A US uranium mine's operating systems. Finally a US item, and I wish it were not.

analyst.briefing: The Peninsula filing is the one to read twice: 'a breach of its operating system' with administrative systems explicitly unaffected is a company drawing the IT/OT line in public and putting the incident on the OT side; an in-situ recovery uranium project runs wellfield pumps and process plants on SCADA, so loss of those systems means a stop (SecurityWeek, 2026-11-24). I hold attribution at unknown and confidence moderate until the Nov 25 announcement. KEPCO is IT: two customer-facing systems, data theft, extortion; the interesting field is the supplier system, because contractor identities are the map an OT intruder wants (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-23). The Norwegian case is a platform flaw: APIM Classic instances leaked the secrets that front integrations, and in an energy company those integrations reach historians, market APIs and DER platforms (The Register, 2026-11-23). Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA now has a public unauthenticated RCE, CVSS 9.8 (CISA, 2026-11-24); [inference] it is the controller family Danfoss said was involved in the European refrigeration attacks, but the advisory does not say this flaw was the one used. NVD confirms CVSS 9.3 for CVE-2026-129713; it is not in KEV.

answers.Who is likely behind the main incident a: Nobody is named by any government or responder this week. KEPCO's attacker is a self-styled 'Noiem', a claim via a Korean outlet (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-23). Peninsula, Norway and Osaki are unattributed. Confidence in any attribution: none to offer.
answers.Did any attack actually reach operationa: Peninsula says yes in effect: operating systems breached, administrative systems not, operations affected (SecurityWeek, 2026-11-24). Osaki's production lines stopped (Industrial Cyber, 2026-11-24). KEPCO and Norway are IT.
answers.What should a utility security team do t: Rotate every secret held in Azure APIM Classic and audit admin operations since Nov 18 (The Register, 2026-11-23). Patch Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA past 5.4.0 and change AK-SC 355 passwords (CISA, 2026-11-24; INCIBE, 2026-11-23). Retire SonicWall Gen 6 from the internet edge (The Hacker News, 2026-11-20). Read Peninsula's Nov 25 announcement for the IT/OT answer.

analyst.bubble: 'Operating system', not 'administrative'. That is the company drawing the OT line.

critic.briefing: Source quality was unusually good this week. Two of the four incidents rest on victim statements (Peninsula's exchange filing, KEPCO's newsroom), one on a national security authority (Norway's NSM), and the advisories come from CISA directly, whose feed answered us for the first time (CISA, 2026-11-24). The weak links: the Osaki story reaches us only through Industrial Cyber relaying an OT-ISAC report, and Industrial Cyber blocks our puller, so an ISAC's finding is cited at second hand (Industrial Cyber, 2026-11-24); the KEPCO attacker name comes from a Korean outlet via BleepingComputer; and The Register's Norway piece relies on a non-public Microsoft advisory it has seen but we have not (The Register, 2026-11-23). Vendor framing to watch: SonicWall's 'AI-assisted attackers' line sells replacement firewalls while being, on this week's evidence from the UK NCSC and OpenAI's pipeline, probably true (The Hacker News, 2026-11-20; CyberScoop, 2026-11-24).

answers.What is the bias of each source covering: CISA: primary, authoritative, and finally readable by us. SecurityWeek and BleepingComputer: fast, incident-driven, both quoting the victims' own statements this week. The Register: sceptical, relying on a non-public Microsoft document. Industrial Cyber: vendor-advertising-funded OT trade press that blocks automated readers. Security.NL and INCIBE: independent and government relays in Dutch and Spanish, consistent with CISA on Danfoss.
answers.Is any story being driven by a vendor's: SonicWall's retirement notice is a vendor telling customers to buy new hardware, however justified (The Hacker News, 2026-11-20). The Mythos feature in Industrial Cyber is a trade outlet writing about a vendor's product (Industrial Cyber, 2026-11-24). Everything else originates with victims or governments.
answers.How does the US coverage differ from int: US coverage this week is thin and institutional (the uranium mine, a personnel change). The incidents with detail are abroad: Korea, Norway, Japan, all through English-language outlets plus Dutch and Spanish relays. The Osaki report exists in an ISAC we cannot read.

critic.bubble: Victim statements and CISA this week. The weak link is a trade outlet that blocks us.

wideangle.briefing: Three things outside energy press in on it. First, AI and exploitation: the UK NCSC and threat companies report a marked rise in AI-assisted hacks (CyberScoop, 2026-11-24; The Record, 2026-11-24), OpenAI shipped a cyber-focused model with stated rules of engagement (CyberScoop; The Register, Nov 24 per the wide bucket), and Anthropic expanded safeguards for detecting AI misuse (SecurityWeek, 2026-11-24); SonicWall's end-of-life notice cites exactly this (The Hacker News, 2026-11-20). Second, edge and platform flaws: VMware vCenter has another critical auth bypass after zero-day exploitation (The Hacker News, 2026-11-24), Check Point servers were compromised at 22 organizations (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-24), CISA flagged an exploited N-able flaw (The Record, 2026-11-24), and Codesys, which underpins many PLC runtimes, has a control-systems advisory from Canada's cyber centre (CCCS, 2026-11-24). Third, load: TVA signed a $1.7 billion data-centre deal under a new large-load tariff and Vistra's CEO says the midterms clarified data-centre development (Utility Dive, 2026-11-24), which is the Technologist's beat and the data-centre dossier's reason to exist.

answers.What else happened in cyberspace today t: VMware vCenter and Check Point exploitation, an exploited N-able flaw, and a Codesys advisory: the virtualization, perimeter, RMM and PLC-runtime layers all at once (The Hacker News; BleepingComputer; The Record; CCCS, all 2026-11-24).
answers.Any new zero-days or ransomware waves en: vCenter auth bypass (9.8) after a zero-day, N-able in KEV, and the Danfoss RCE on the energy side; Danfoss and Zyxel's CVEs are still not in KEV per today's check.
answers.Is there a geopolitical angle this week?: Not in this bundle beyond the Norwegian case, where the state security authority spoke; the AI-capability stories are industrial policy, not conflict.

wideangle.bubble: vCenter, Check Point, N-able, Codesys, Danfoss. The edge is leaking everywhere this week.

contrarian.briefing: Who was not affected: every US grid operator, pipeline and refinery, in a week when the sector abroad took real hits. The one US incident is a uranium mine whose filing says 'operating system' without saying which, and I will not let 'OT' be assumed; a company that separates administrative systems from an unnamed operating system may be describing a process network or may be describing a plant server (SecurityWeek, 2026-11-24). KEPCO lost 1.5 million records and not one electron; generation, transmission and distribution were untouched, and the headline number may double-count people who are both customers and employees (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-23). Norway: two energy companies 'affected' by a platform flaw is not two energy companies breached; the extent is 'unclear' by the outlet's own words (The Register, 2026-11-23). What the coverage is not telling us: whether any of the hundreds of APIM Classic users in the US energy sector were touched, and whether Osaki's halted lines mean a single utility short of meters.

answers.Who was not affected by today's main inc: Every US grid operator; every European utility except the two Norwegian companies, and those only through a cloud flaw; every KEPCO physical system. The reason is unglamorous: these attacks went where the data and the secrets were, not where the switches are.
answers.Is the impact being overstated anywhere?: KEPCO's 1.5 million may overlap across the three groups (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-23). 'Two major energy companies' in Norway is the number affected, not breached. Peninsula 'temporarily affect its operations' is the company's phrase; no production figure exists.
answers.What is the coverage not telling us?: The Osaki report itself, which we cannot read. The Peninsula follow-up due Nov 25. Whether the Danfoss RCE was ever used in the autumn attacks, which nobody has said.

contrarian.bubble: 'Operating system' is a phrase. I want to see the Nov 25 filing.

summary.headline: Four confirmed energy incidents in a week: a US uranium mine's operating systems, KEPCO's 1.5 million records, two Norwegian majors through an Azure flaw, and a smart-meter maker's lines; plus the refrigeration controllers' flaws finally published.

bullets.text: Peninsula Energy halted ASX trading after a cyber incident breached the operating systems at its Lance uranium project in Wyoming; administrative systems unaffected; announcement due Nov 25.

KEPCO confirmed a breach of its billing portal and procurement system: about 1.5 million customer, representative and employee records; Korea's privacy regulator confirmed an extortion email; no OT effect.

Norway's NSM linked attacks on two major energy companies, naming Equinor and Skagerak Energi, to a critical Azure API Management Classic flaw; Microsoft mitigated Nov 19; assume secrets exposed and rotate.
Ransomware at Osaki Electric disrupted smart-meter production; OT-ISAC warns of supplier continuity risk across Asia-Pacific.

Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA refrigeration controllers: CISA advisory for a CVSS 9.8 unauthenticated RCE (CVE-2026-129713), and INCIBE on default credentials in AK-SC 355 / AK-SM 800: the controller family named in the autumn's European attacks.
GL.iNet's cloud management flaw was exploited to put malware on routers and KVMs; SonicWall told customers to retire Gen 6 firewalls, which will get no more patches.
AI moved from forecast to product: OpenAI shipped a cyber model with rules of engagement, the UK NCSC reports a marked rise in AI-assisted attacks, Anthropic expanded misuse safeguards.
US: the national cyber director left office during the lame-duck session that decides the CISA 2015 sunset; TVA signed a $1.7 billion data-centre deal under a new large-load tariff.

considerations: The first confirmed US energy-production incident on the board rests on one filing's phrase, 'operating system'; the Analyst reads OT, the Contrarian will not assume it. The Nov 25 announcement settles it.
Where the attacks went: data and secrets (KEPCO, Norway), not switches. OT contact this week is a mine and a factory, not a grid.
The Danfoss advisories are the public end of the autumn's refrigeration story, but no document says these flaws were the ones used; the link is inference and labelled.
